claim: Morphine is a potent analgesic with high addictive potential.
source: Morphine is a potent analgesic with high addictive potential.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about morphine's pharmacological properties.

claim: Morphine-induced addictive behaviors are strongly dependent on the activation of dopamine (DA) neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Morphine-induced addictive behaviors are strongly dependent on the activation of dopamine (DA) neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Wise, 1989; Gardner, 2011; Luscher and Malenka, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The hedonic response produced by the activation of VTA-DA neurons by morphine is a primary factor behind drug dependence.
source: The hedonic response produced by the activation of VTA-DA neurons by morphine is a primary factor behind drug dependence.
evidence: This is an inference based on established understanding of reward circuitry and drug dependence.

claim: One previously reported mechanism for morphine activation of VTA-DA neurons is the VTA-DA neuron disinhibition model.
source: One previously reported mechanism for morphine activation of VTA-DA neurons is the VTA-DA neuron disinhibition model (Johnson and North, 1992; Kalivas, 1993; White, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Morphine first inhibits neighboring GABA inhibitory neurons, which shifts the balance between inhibitory and excitatory input to VTA-DA neurons in favor of excitation and then leads to the promotion of VTA-DA neuron excitation.
source: Morphine first inhibits neighboring GABA inhibitory neurons, which shifts the balance between inhibitory and excitatory input to VTA-DA neurons in favor of excitation and then leads to the promotion of VTA-DA neuron excitation.
evidence: This describes the disinhibition model mechanism based on prior literature.

claim: The release of glutamate from at least some of the glutamate terminals that synapsed on VTA-DA neurons was inhibited by opioids.
source: It was also reported that the release of glutamate from least some of the glutamate terminals that synapsed on VTA-DA neurons was inhibited by opioids (Manzoni and Williams, 1999; Margolis et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The inhibitory effect of opioids on glutamate release is puzzling.
source: This inhibitory effect of opioids on glutamate release is puzzling (Chartoff and Connery, 2014) because one would expect morphine to produce rapid activation of VTA-DA neurons through both the inhibition of GABAergic input and the excitation of glutamatergic input.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the expected effects of morphine, with citation support.

claim: Postsynaptic inhibition in response to μ opioid receptor activation has been reported in some VTA-DA neurons.
source: In addition, postsynaptic inhibition (Ford et al., 2006) or excitation (Margolis et al., 2014) in response to μ opioid receptor activation has also been reported in some VTA-DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Postsynaptic excitation in response to μ opioid receptor activation has been reported in some VTA-DA neurons.
source: In addition, postsynaptic inhibition (Ford et al., 2006) or excitation (Margolis et al., 2014) in response to μ opioid receptor activation has also been reported in some VTA-DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The amplitude of the inhibitory outward currents produced by opioids in postsynaptic VTA-DA neurons was small (2.1 ± 1.5 pA in VTA-DA neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens and 14 ± 4 pA in those projecting to the basolateral amygdaloid nucleus).
source: However, the amplitude of the inhibitory outward currents produced by opioids in postsynaptic VTA-DA neurons in the study of Ford et al. was small (2.1 ± 1.5 pA in VTA-DA neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens and 14 ± 4 pA in those projecting to the basolateral amygdaloid nucleus) (Ford et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research data.

claim: Only a small population of VTA-DA neurons (19%) showed depolarization or an increase in firing rate in response to opioids.
source: while only a small population of VTA-DA neurons (19%) showed depolarization or an increase in firing rate in response to opioids in the study of Margolis et al. (2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research data.

claim: Only a few VTA-DA neurons had µ receptors.
source: This low postsynaptic responsiveness to opioids was consistent with physiological and anatomical evidence that only a few VTA-DA neurons had µ receptors (Ford et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Blockade of excitatory glutamatergic signaling in the VTA suppressed morphine-induced VTA-DA neuron activation.
source: Here, we propose that morphine might have a strengthening, rather than an inhibitory, effect on glutamatergic input to VTA-DA neurons because it was reported that blockade of excitatory glutamatergic signaling in the VTA suppressed morphine-induced VTA-DA neuron activation (Jalabert et al., 2011) and related behaviors (Kalivas and Alesdatter, 1993; Harris and Aston-Jones, 2003; Harris et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Blockade of excitatory glutamatergic signaling in the VTA suppressed morphine-induced behaviors related to VTA-DA neuron activation.
source: Here, we propose that morphine might have a strengthening, rather than an inhibitory, effect on glutamatergic input to VTA-DA neurons because it was reported that blockade of excitatory glutamatergic signaling in the VTA suppressed morphine-induced VTA-DA neuron activation (Jalabert et al., 2011) and related behaviors (Kalivas and Alesdatter, 1993; Harris and Aston-Jones, 2003; Harris et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VTA-DA neurons were identified based on Ih currents and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) staining.
source: VTA-DA neurons were identified based on Ih currents (Figure 1A) and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) staining (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Morphine (10 μM) increased the frequency of spontaneous firing in VTA-DA neurons.
source: Using original recordings of spontaneous firing (left panel of Figure 2A) and the time course of spontaneous firing (middle panel of Figure 2A) in VTA-DA neurons for comparison, we could see that morphine (10 μM) increased the frequency of spontaneous firing in VTA-DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The average frequency of spontaneous firing increased from 1.0 ± 0.3 Hz before to 1.4 ± 0.4 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from five rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average frequency of spontaneous firing increased from 1.0 ± 0.3 Hz before to 1.4 ± 0.4 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from five rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before morphine, right panel of Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of APV and DNQX, morphine no longer increased spontaneous firing frequency.
source: In the presence of APV and DNQX, morphine no longer increased spontaneous firing frequency (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average frequency of spontaneous firing was 0.7 ± 0.1 Hz before and 0.8 ± 0.1 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application in the presence of APV and DNQX (n = 6 cells from five rats, paired t test, p > 0.05).
source: The average frequency of spontaneous firing was 0.7 ± 0.1 Hz before and 0.8 ± 0.1 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application in the presence of APV and DNQX (n = 6 cells from five rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to control with APV and DNQX before morphine, right panel of Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The morphine-induced increase in the spontaneous firing frequency of VTA-DA neurons requires AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated glutamatergic input.
source: These results suggest that the morphine-induced increase in the spontaneous firing frequency of VTA-DA neurons requires AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated glutamatergic input, consistent with a recent report using the NMDA antagonist APV and the AMPA receptor antagonist 6-Cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2, 3-dione (CNQX) in in vivo experiments (Jalabert et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: In the presence of extracellularly applied PTX (100 μM), morphine (10 μM) decreased the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: Consistent with earlier reports (Manzoni and Williams, 1999; Margolis et al., 2005), in the presence of extracellularly applied PTX (100 μM), morphine (10 μM) decreased the frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: The average frequency of sEPSCs decreased from 4.2 ± 0.7 Hz before to 3.5 ± 0.7 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application in the presence of extracellularly applied PTX (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average frequency of sEPSCs decreased from 4.2 ± 0.7 Hz before to 3.5 ± 0.7 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before morphine, right panel of Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Intracellularly applied PTX (100 μM) blocked IPSCs in VTA-DA neurons.
source: The results showed that under this experimental paradigm, IPSCs disappeared (top of panel 1 in Figure 3B, n = 5 cells from two rats), demonstrating that GABAA receptors in the recorded VTA-DA neurons were blocked by intracellularly applied PTX.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spontaneous events in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX were completely blocked by DNQX (10 μM).
source: The results showed that the spontaneous events were completely blocked by DNQX (10 μM) (bottom of panel 1 in Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Morphine (10 μM) increased the frequency of sEPSCs in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX.
source: Raw current traces (panel 2 of Figure 3B) and the time course of sEPSCs (panel 3 of Figure 3B) before and after morphine application in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX showed that morphine (10 μM) increased the frequency of sEPSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average frequency of sEPSCs increased from 4.8 ± 0.6 Hz before to 5.5 ± 0.6 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX (n = 8 cells from five rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average frequency of sEPSCs increased from 4.8 ± 0.6 Hz before to 5.5 ± 0.6 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 8 cells from five rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before morphine, panel 4 of Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine (10 μM) had no significant effect on the amplitude of sEPSCs in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX.
source: However, morphine (10 μM) had no significant effect on the amplitude of sEPSCs. The average amplitude of sEPSCs was 16.6 ± 1.3 pA before and 15.3 ± 1.3 pA for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 8 cells from five rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to control before morphine, panel 5 of Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine (10 μM) increased the amplitude of the first EPSC in paired pulse facilitation experiments.
source: As shown in the left panel of Figure 3C, morphine (10 μM) increased the amplitude of the first EPSC, which was accompanied by a clear change in the presynaptic parameter PPF.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average amplitude of the first EPSCs was 124.1 ± 9.0 pA before and 161.9 ± 10.8 pA for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average amplitude of the first EPSCs was 124.1 ± 9.0 pA before and 161.9 ± 10.8 pA for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before morphine, middle panel of Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The average PPF was decreased from 1.5 ± 0.2 before to 1.2 ± 0.1 for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average PPF was decreased from 1.5 ± 0.2 before to 1.2 ± 0.1 for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before morphine, right panel of Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine increased presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX.
source: These results supported the suggestion that morphine increased presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons in the presence of intracellularly applied PTX.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on sEPSC frequency and PPF.

claim: When the membrane potential of VTA-DA neurons was clamped at the reversal potential of Cl− channels, morphine exerted a promoting effect on presynaptic glutamate release.
source: More importantly, when we clamped the membrane potential of VTA-DA neurons at the reversal potential of Cl− channels to remove sIPSCs, as an alternative to the application of a GABAA antagonist, either by the intracellular or bath approach, morphine still exerted a promoting effect on presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The average frequency of sEPSCs increased from 4.4 ± 0.3 Hz before to 5.5 ± 0.4 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application when VTA-DA neurons were clamped at the reversal potential of Cl− channels (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average frequency of sEPSCs in this condition increased from 4.4 ± 0.3 Hz before to 5.5 ± 0.4 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before morphine, right panel of Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine (10 μM) had no significant effect on glutamate release from VTA synaptosomes.
source: However, we did not find that morphine (10 μM) had a direct effect at glutamatergic terminals to promote glutamate release. The average concentration of glutamate was 8.1 ± 0.1 nmol/mg before and 8.5 ± 0.7 nmol/mg after morphine application (n = 6 samples from eight rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine (10 µM) had no significant effect on the frequency of sEPSCs from mechanically dissociated single VTA-DA neurons.
source: The results showed that morphine (10 µM) had no significant effect on the frequency of sEPSCs (panels 2 and 3 of Figure 4B). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 2.1 ± 0.3 Hz before and 2.0 ± 0.2 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application (10 µM) (n = 6 cells from six rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to control before morphine, panel 4 of Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine may promote presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons in an indirect way.
source: These results suggest that morphine may promote presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons in an indirect way.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing no direct effect on synaptosomes or dissociated neurons.

claim: GABA (10 μM) decreased the frequency of sEPSCs in VTA-DA neurons.
source: From raw current traces (left panel of Figure 5A) and the time course of sEPSCs (middle panel of Figure 5A), we could see that GABA (10 μM) apparently decreased the frequency of sEPSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The average frequency of sEPSCs decreased from 6.7 ± 0.7 Hz before to 4.7 ± 0.6 Hz for 10–15 min after GABA application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average frequency of sEPSCs decreased from 6.7 ± 0.7 Hz before to 4.7 ± 0.6 Hz for 10–15 min after GABA application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before GABA, right panel of Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: 470 nm light stimulation (20 Hz) elicited action potentials in GABA neurons expressing ChR2.
source: The results showed that 470 nm light stimulation (20 Hz) elicited action potentials in GABA neurons (panel 2 of Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 470 nm light stimulation decreased the frequency of sEPSCs in VTA-DA neurons.
source: Raw current traces (panel 3 of Figure 5B) and the time course of sEPSCs (panel 4 of Figure 5B) before and after light stimulation showed that the light stimulation apparently decreased the frequency of sEPSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The average frequency of sEPSCs decreased from 4.1 ± 0.7 Hz before to 2.7 ± 0.3 Hz for 10–15 min after 470 nm light stimulation (n = 6 cells from five mice, paired t test, p < 0.05).
source: The average frequency of sEPSCs decreased from 4.1 ± 0.7 Hz before to 2.7 ± 0.3 Hz for 10–15 min after light stimulation (n = 6 cells from five mice, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before light stimulation, panel 5 of Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The GABAA receptor antagonist PTX (100 µM) had no significant influence on the effect of GABA on the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: The results showed that the GABAA receptor antagonist PTX (100 µM) had no significant influence on the effect of GABA (Figure 6A). The average frequency of sEPSCs still decreased from 4.0 ± 0.3 Hz before to 3.0 ± 0.2 Hz for 10–15 min after GABA application in the presence of PTX (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to PTX before GABA, right panel of Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of the GABAB receptor antagonist CGP54626, the effect of GABA on the frequency of sEPSCs disappeared.
source: However, in the presence of the GABAB receptor antagonist CGP54626, the effect of GABA on the frequency of sEPSCs disappeared (Figure 6B). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 3.8 ± 0.4 Hz before and 3.8 ± 0.4 Hz for 10–15 min after GABA application in the presence of CGP54626 (2 µM) (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to CGP54626 before GABA, right panel of Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: GABAB receptors, rather than GABAA receptors, mediate the decreasing effect of GABA on presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons.
source: These results suggest that it is GABAB receptors, rather than GABAA receptors, that mediate the decreasing effect of GABA on presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing differential effects of GABAA and GABAB antagonists.

claim: The inhibitory effect of 470 nm light stimulation on the frequency of sEPSCs disappeared in the presence of CGP54626.
source: From raw current traces (left panel of Figure 6C) and the time course of sEPSCs (middle panel of Figure 6C) before and after the 470 nm light stimulation in the presence of CGP54626 (2 µM), we could see that the inhibitory effect of the 470 nm light stimulation on the frequency of sEPSCs disappeared in the presence of CGP54626.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The average frequency of sEPSCs was 4.2 ± 0.3 Hz before and 4.1 ± 0.2 Hz for 10–15 min after 470 nm light stimulation in the presence of CGP54626 (n = 6 cells from five mice, paired t test, p > 0.05).
source: The average frequency of sEPSCs was 4.2 ± 0.3 Hz before and 4.1 ± 0.2 Hz for 10–15 min after 470 nm light stimulation in the presence of CGP54626 (n = 6 cells from five mice, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to control before 470 nm light stimulation in the presence of CGP54626, right panel of Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: GABAB receptors were present in synaptosomes from the VTA.
source: Western blotting indicated that GABAB receptors were present in synaptosomes from the VTA (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: GABAB receptors were present in glutamatergic terminals of the VTA.
source: Immunohistochemistry results for GABAB receptors, VGLUT2 (a glutamatergic terminal marker) and TH (a DA neuron marker) showed that GABAB receptors (green color, panel 1 of Figure 7B), VGLUT2 (red color, panel 2 of Figure 7B) and TH-positive neurons (blue color, panel 3 of Figure 7B) were present in VTA slices and the coexpression of GABAB receptors and VGLUT2 (yellow color, panel 4 of Figure 7B) indicated that GABAB receptors were present in glutamatergic terminals of the VTA in rats.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The coexpression of GABAB receptors and VGLUT2 was close to TH-positive neurons.
source: Moreover, this coexpression was close to TH-positive neurons (panel 4 of Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The GABAB receptor antagonist CGP54626 increased the frequency of sEPSCs in VTA-DA neurons.
source: The results showed that after the application of CGP54626, the frequency of sEPSCs significantly increased (Figure 8A). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 3.6 ± 0.3 Hz before and 4.5 ± 0.3 Hz for 10–15 min after CGP54626 application (2 µM) (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before CGP54626, right panel of Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The GABAA receptor antagonist PTX had no significant effect on the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: However, the GABAA receptor antagonist PTX had no significant effect on the frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 8B). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 5.8 ± 1.0 Hz before and 5.7 ± 0.9 Hz for 10–15 min after PTX (100 µM) application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to control before PTX, right panel of Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There is basal GABAergic inhibitory control through GABAB receptors on presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons.
source: In addition, to determine whether there is basal GABAergic inhibitory control through GABAB receptors on presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons, we observed the effect of the GABAB receptor antagonist CGP54626 on the frequency of sEPSCs in rats. The results showed that after the application of CGP54626, the frequency of sEPSCs significantly increased (Figure 8A).
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing CGP54626 increases sEPSC frequency.

claim: Yellow light stimulation (590 nm) could reliably inhibit the current injection-induced firing of action potentials in GABA neurons expressing eNpHR3.0.
source: The results showed that yellow light stimulation (590 nm) could reliably inhibit the current injection-induced firing of action potentials in GABA neurons (left panel of Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Yellow light stimulation (590 nm) increased the frequency of sEPSCs in VTA-DA neurons.
source: As expected, light stimulation increased the frequency of sEPSCs in VTA-DA neurons (middle panel of Figure 9A). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 3.9 ± 0.4 Hz before and 4.5 ± 0.4 Hz for 10–15 min after light stimulation (n = 6 cells from five mice, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before light stimulation, right panel of Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of morphine on the frequency of sEPSCs disappeared in the presence of 590 nm light stimulation.
source: From raw current traces (left panel of Figure 9B) and the time course of sEPSCs (middle panel of Figure 9B), we could see that the effect of morphine on the frequency of sEPSCs disappeared in the presence of the light stimulation. The average frequency of sEPSCs was 4.5 ± 0.4 Hz before and 4.4 ± 0.5 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application in the presence of the light stimulation (n = 6 cells from five mice, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to control before morphine with light stimulation, right panel of Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine promotes presynaptic glutamate release of VTA-DA neurons via presynaptic disinhibition.
source: These results suggest that prior removal of the inhibition of GABAergic input on presynaptic glutamate release leads to disappearance of the effect of morphine on presynaptic glutamate release of VTA-DA neurons, indicating that morphine promotes presynaptic glutamate release of VTA-DA neurons via presynaptic disinhibition.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing light-induced disinhibition abolishes morphine's effect.

claim: After application of the GABAB receptor antagonist CGP54626 (2 µM), the frequency of sEPSCs significantly increased.
source: The results showed that after application of the GABAB receptor antagonist CGP54626 (2 µM), the frequency of sEPSCs significantly increased (Figure 9C). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 2.5 ± 0.4 Hz before and 3.0 ± 0.4 Hz for 5–10 min after CGP54626 application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before CGP54626, right panel of Figure 9C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Morphine (10 µM) did not further increase the frequency of sEPSCs in the presence of CGP54626.
source: On this basis, morphine (10 µM) was applied in the same cell, but did not further increase the frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 9C). The average frequency of sEPSCs was 3.0 ± 0.4 Hz before and 2.8 ± 0.4 Hz for 5–10 min after morphine application in the presence of CGP54626 (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to CGP54626 before morphine, right panel of Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: CGP36216 (100 µM) increased the frequency of spontaneous firing in VTA-DA neurons.
source: The results showed that CGP36216 (100 µM) could increase the frequency of spontaneous firing in VTA-DA neurons (Figure 10A). The average frequency of spontaneous firing increased from 1.8 ± 0.3 Hz before to 2.1 ± 0.3 Hz after CGP36216 application (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p < 0.05, compared to control before CGP36216, right panel of Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of morphine (10 µM) on spontaneous firing frequency disappeared in the presence of CGP36216 (100 µM).
source: As shown by raw spontaneous firing traces (left panel of Figure 10B) and the time course of spontaneous firing (middle panel of Figure 10B) in VTA-DA neurons, the effect of morphine (10 µM) disappeared in the presence of CGP36216 (100 µM). The average frequency of spontaneous firing in VTA-DA neurons was 1.3 ± 0.2 Hz before and 1.2 ± 0.2 Hz for 10–15 min after morphine application in the presence of CGP36216 (n = 6 cells from four rats, paired t test, p > 0.05, compared to CGP36216 before morphine, right panel of Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: CGP36216 (20 μg/rat) increased locomotor activity in rats.
source: The results showed that CGP36216 (20 μg/rat) increased locomotor activity. The distance traveled by rats was 6.3 ± 1.4 m in the control group compared with 12.2 ± 2.0 m in the CGP36216 group (n = 6 rats, independent t test, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Locomotor activity was significantly increased following intra-VTA injection of morphine (1 µg/rat).
source: As shown in Figure 11B, locomotor activity was significantly increased following intra-VTA injection of morphine (1 µg/rat). The distance traveled by rats was 6.3 ± 1.4 m in the control group compared with 37.6 ± 9.6 m in the morphine alone group (n = 6 rats, independent t test, p < 0.05, right panel of Figure 11B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In animals with intra-VTA injection of CGP36216 (20 µg/rat), the morphine-induced increase in locomotor activity disappeared.
source: However, in animals with intra-VTA injection of CGP36216 (20 µg/rat), the morphine-induced increase in locomotor activity disappeared (Figure 11B). The distance traveled by rats was 37.6 ± 9.6 m in the morphine alone group compared with 7.5 ± 1.4 m in the morphine plus intra-VTA CGP36216 group (n = 6 rats, independent t test, p < 0.05, right panel of Figure 11B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Locomotor activity was significantly increased by i.p. injection of morphine (10 mg/kg) plus intra-VTA injection of saline.
source: As shown in Figure 11C, locomotor activity was significantly increased by i.p. injection of morphine (10 mg/kg) plus intra-VTA injection of saline. The distance traveled by rats was 5.4 ± 0.8 m in the control group compared with 28.3 ± 5.7 m in the i.p. morphine (10 mg/kg) plus intra-VTA saline group (n = 6 rats, independent t test, p < 0.05, right panel of Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In animals with intra-VTA injection of CGP36216 (20 µg/rat), the i.p. morphine-induced increase in locomotor activity disappeared.
source: However, in animals with intra-VTA injection of CGP36216 (20 µg/rat), the i.p. morphine-induced increase in locomotor activity disappeared (Figure 11C). The distance traveled by rats was 28.3 ± 5.7 m in the i.p. morphine (10 mg/kg) plus intra-VTA saline group compared with 6.6 ± 2.3 m in the i.p. morphine plus intra-VTA CGP36216 group (n = 6 rats, independent t test, p < 0.05, right panel of Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: After CPP training, the morphine group exhibited greater CPP compared with the control group.
source: Post-hoc analysis showed that after CPP training, the morphine group (n = 6 rats) exhibited greater CPP compared with the control group (n = 6 rats, p < 0.05) but in groups receiving CGP36216 (n = 6 rats), morphine-induced CPP was absent (p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In groups receiving CGP36216, morphine-induced CPP was absent.
source: Post-hoc analysis showed that after CPP training, the morphine group (n = 6 rats) exhibited greater CPP compared with the control group (n = 6 rats, p < 0.05) but in groups receiving CGP36216 (n = 6 rats), morphine-induced CPP was absent (p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Intra-VTA injection of a presynaptic GABAB receptor antagonist abolishes CPP induced by intra-VTA injection of morphine.
source: These results suggest that intra-VTA injection of a presynaptic GABAB receptor antagonist abolishes CPP induced by intra-VTA injection of morphine.
evidence: Inference from behavioral experimental data on CPP.

claim: The disinhibitory action of morphine on presynaptic glutamate release might be the main mechanism for morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron firing and related behaviors.
source: Our results suggest that the disinhibitory action of morphine on presynaptic glutamate release might be the main mechanism for morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron firing and related behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including electrophysiology and behavior.

claim: Glutamatergic input to VTA-DA neurons is inhibited by GABAergic interneurons via GABAB receptors.
source: Our results suggest that glutamatergic input to VTA-DA neurons is inhibited by GABAergic interneurons via GABAB receptors and that morphine promotes presynaptic glutamate release by removing this inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental results showing GABA inhibits glutamate release via GABAB receptors.

claim: Morphine promotes presynaptic glutamate release by removing GABAergic inhibition.
source: Our results suggest that glutamatergic input to VTA-DA neurons is inhibited by GABAergic interneurons via GABAB receptors and that morphine promotes presynaptic glutamate release by removing this inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental results showing morphine's effect is abolished when GABAergic inhibition is removed.

claim: Under the condition of bath application of a GABAA receptor antagonist, morphine produced an inhibitory effect on the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: We believe that under the condition of bath application of a GABAA receptor antagonist, the antagonist can produce a wide inhibitory effect on GABAA receptors present on various neuron subtypes, such as DA neurons and GABA neurons, in VTA slices. Maybe this wide effect shifts the effect of morphine on presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons toward an inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the different effects observed with different application methods.

claim: The intracellular application of a GABAA receptor antagonist only blocks GABAA receptors in the single VTA-DA neuron being recorded.
source: However, the intracellular application of a GABAA receptor antagonist only blocks GABAA receptors in the single VTA-DA neuron being recorded.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of how intracellular application works.

claim: µ receptors located in GABAergic interneurons are the primary site of action of opiates in the VTA.
source: It has been proposed that µ receptors located in GABAergic interneurons are the primary site of action of opiates in the VTA (Hyman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: µ receptors are primarily located on non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA.
source: This is consistent with morphological and functional data showing that µ receptors are primarily located on non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA (Garzon and Pickel, 2001) and that activation of µ receptors can inhibit GABAergic interneurons by hyperpolarizing the cells (Johnson and North, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activation of µ receptors can inhibit GABAergic interneurons by hyperpolarizing the cells.
source: This is consistent with morphological and functional data showing that µ receptors are primarily located on non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA (Garzon and Pickel, 2001) and that activation of µ receptors can inhibit GABAergic interneurons by hyperpolarizing the cells (Johnson and North, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There was a positive correlation between basal dopamine levels and the glutamate/GABA ratio in the VTA of wild-type animals.
source: They found that there was a positive correlation between basal dopamine levels and the glutamate/GABA ratio in the VTA of wild-type animals.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Chefer et al. study.

claim: In µ receptor knockout mice, the GABAergic inhibitory tone in the VTA was significantly increased.
source: Moreover, in µ receptor knockout mice, the GABAergic inhibitory tone in the VTA was significantly increased, but the glutamatergic excitatory tone was decreased.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Chefer et al. study.

claim: In µ receptor knockout mice, the glutamatergic excitatory tone in the VTA was decreased.
source: Moreover, in µ receptor knockout mice, the GABAergic inhibitory tone in the VTA was significantly increased, but the glutamatergic excitatory tone was decreased.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Chefer et al. study.

claim: The µ receptor antagonist CTOP can block the promoting effect of morphine on the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: This is supported by our results indicating that the µ receptor antagonist CTOP can block the promoting effect of morphine on the frequency of sEPSCs (the average frequency of sEPSCs was 2.95 ± 0.35 Hz before and 2.97 ± 0.40 after morphine application (10 µM) in the presence of CTOP (1 µM); n = 6 cells from four rats, p > 0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Pre- and postsynaptic GABAB receptors in central neurons may be pharmacologically distinct.
source: Several studies have indicated that pre- and postsynaptic GABAB receptors in central neurons may be pharmacologically distinct (Dutar and Nicoll, 1988; Deisz et al., 1993, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CGP36216 is a useful lead compound to differentiate between pre- and postsynaptic GABAB receptors.
source: CGP36216 is a useful lead compound to differentiate between pre- and postsynaptic GABAB receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacological properties of CGP36216.

claim: Up to 1 mM of CGP36216 was ineffective in antagonizing baclofen-induced hyperpolarization mediated through postsynaptic GABAB receptors.
source: Up to 1 mM of CGP36216 was ineffective in antagonizing baclofen-induced hyperpolarization mediated through postsynaptic GABAB receptors, but the responses mediated through presynaptic GABAB receptors were reversibly antagonized by CGP36216 with an IC50 of 43 µM (Ong et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The responses mediated through presynaptic GABAB receptors were reversibly antagonized by CGP36216 with an IC50 of 43 µM.
source: Up to 1 mM of CGP36216 was ineffective in antagonizing baclofen-induced hyperpolarization mediated through postsynaptic GABAB receptors, but the responses mediated through presynaptic GABAB receptors were reversibly antagonized by CGP36216 with an IC50 of 43 µM (Ong et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: If GABAergic inhibitory control of presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons was removed, the effect of morphine on the firing of VTA-DA neurons disappeared.
source: Our results showed that if GABAergic inhibitory control of presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons was removed, the effect of morphine on the firing of VTA-DA neurons disappeared, indicating that the morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron activity might mainly depend on its disinhibitory action on presynaptic glutamate release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing CGP36216 abolishes morphine's effect on firing.

claim: The morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron activity might mainly depend on its disinhibitory action on presynaptic glutamate release.
source: Our results showed that if GABAergic inhibitory control of presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons was removed, the effect of morphine on the firing of VTA-DA neurons disappeared, indicating that the morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron activity might mainly depend on its disinhibitory action on presynaptic glutamate release.
evidence: This is an inference from experimental data.

claim: Increased VTA-DA neuron activity is often assessed as increased locomotor activity at the behavioral level.
source: We also observe the effect of removing GABA inhibitory control of presynaptic glutamate release with the presynaptic GABAB receptor antagonist CGP36216 on morphine-induced increase in locomotor activity, which is often assessed as increased VTA-DA neuron activity at the behavioral level (Vezina, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Intra-VTA injection of a presynaptic GABAB receptor antagonist could abolish the increase in rat locomotor activity induced by both i.p. and intra-VTA-injected morphine.
source: The results showed that intra-VTA injection of a presynaptic GABAB receptor antagonist could abolish the increase in rat locomotor activity induced by both i.p. and intra-VTA-injected morphine.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral experimental results.

claim: Morphine-induced CPP is initiated by morphine-induced activation of VTA-DA neurons.
source: In addition, we observed the effect of removing GABA inhibitory control of presynaptic glutamate release with the presynaptic GABAB receptor antagonist CGP36216 on morphine-induced CPP, which is initiated by morphine-induced activation of VTA-DA neurons (Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The disinhibitory action of morphine on presynaptic glutamate release may be the main mechanism in the morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron firing and related behaviors.
source: These data suggest that the disinhibitory action of morphine on presynaptic glutamate release may be the main mechanism in the morphine-induced increase in VTA-DA neuron firing and related behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: 10 µM of morphine is commonly used in in vitro experiments as it elicits a significant effect useful for further analyses.
source: We select 10 µM of morphine because this concentration is commonly used in in vitro experiments as it elicits a significant effect useful for further analyses (Akaishi et al., 2000), and the effect of morphine at this concentration can be essentially abolished by the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone (Valentino and Dingledine, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effect of morphine at 10 µM concentration can be essentially abolished by the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone.
source: We select 10 µM of morphine because this concentration is commonly used in in vitro experiments as it elicits a significant effect useful for further analyses (Akaishi et al., 2000), and the effect of morphine at this concentration can be essentially abolished by the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone (Valentino and Dingledine, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: µ opioid agonists hyperpolarized the GABAergic interneurons of the VTA and reduced the frequency of sIPSCs.
source: It was previously reported that μ-opioid agonists hyperpolarized the GABAergic interneurons of the VTA, reduced the frequency of sIPSCs, and thus produced a disinhibitory action on VTA-DA neurons (Johnson and North, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Morphine disinhibits presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons by a second mechanism in addition to disinhibition of VTA-DA neurons.
source: In the present study, we demonstrated that morphine-disinhibited presynaptic glutamate release in VTA-DA neurons by a second mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of the study.

claim: Both disinhibitory actions (on VTA-DA neurons and on presynaptic glutamate release) may contribute to the morphine-induced excitatory effect on VTA-DA neurons.
source: These two kinds of disinhibitory actions may both contribute to the morphine-induced excitatory effect on VTA-DA neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.
